text: Good afternoon. My name is Lauren Chernov, and I am calling this April 8th, 2026 Specialized Programs and Centers Committee meeting to order. I am joined by my colleague, Mr. John Pepper, and Ms. Donahue has notified us that she will be arriving late today, but we are going to proceed regardless. We have no public comments, so we are going to move to item number 3.01, approval of the draft minutes for the March 4th, 2026 meeting. Are there any changes or additions to the minutes?

Seeing none, I will move for the minutes from March 4th, 2026 meeting to be approved. May I have a second? I'll second that. All in favor? Aye. Aye. Those minutes are approved. We will now move to item number four, which is our only action item this afternoon, 4.01, Hillsboro Charter Academy 2026-2027 school calendar, and I will pass it over to Ms. Layman, who has joined us, and to give any updates

that are necessary. Thank you very much, Chair. You had two questions last month when this was presented. I was able to get clarity on both. First was August 10th and 11th on the HCA calendar are designated as flexible PD days. I learned from Mr. Vickers at HCA that those days are designated to complete the required county trainings, and staff at HCA have the opportunity to complete those any time

prior to those dates, and if they come with them completed those dates, they don't have to work on those two days. If they are not completed, they must be completed on those two days. So that's what flexible means. I asked them to change. The next question was on, it used to say LCPS planning days. And the reason it said when it was actually the 17th and 18th of August, which are LCPS student days, they were trying to designate that those are the required planning days that teachers need to have, and that's when they were happening at

HCA. They start a little bit later than we do. So I said, "Please just reflect what's happening at HCA." And so now it says HCA planning days because that's what those are. So if you have any other questions, I'll try to answer them. I appreciate the update and the answers. Are there any other questions or comments from Mr. Pepper? I was going to say the board members. All right. I don't have any either. Thank you so much for making those changes, and so I will go ahead

and make a motion to send the Hillsboro Charter Academy 2026-2027 school calendar to the full board as an information item. And I second that. All right. It has been properly moved and seconded. All those in favor? Aye. Aye, and that passes unanimously two zero with Ms. Donahue absent for the vote, and that will conclude our action items. So we're moving right along. We have two presentations today for information. We have a special programs update as well as a

career and technical education expansion plan update. So we will go ahead and jump right in with our special programs update. And we have many friends here tonight to present. So I'm actually going to just introduce Ms. Katie Clark, the director of academic programs, and allow her to pass the microphone off as needed. The floor is yours. Awesome. Thank you so much. Good afternoon. We are excited to give you a short update on the program planning and

progress for the Academy of Global and Linguistic Studies, International Baccalaureate, both diploma program at Parkview and the CP program at all three schools, and our expansion to the Army ROTC program. This afternoon, I'm joined by Kelly James, supervisor of world languages and cultures, Danielle Graham, supervisor of social science and global studies, Grant Schaefer, supervisor of academic programs, Rachel Domar,

CTE specialist, and Dr. Grubbs, director of career, technical, and adult education. So first, I'm going to turn it over to Kelly and Danielle to give an update on our planning for the Academy of Global and Linguistic Studies. Thank you. So we are in the midst of our planning year for AGLS. Our wonderful program coordinators spent a lot of time in the fall meeting with all of our middle school students

to inform them and recruit students. We had a lot of students who applied for the program, and they are getting notified about their enrollment and they are enrolling in the program. We're in the midst of our hiring season for next year before we get ready to welcome our first cohort of ninth grade students, with 100 ninth graders anticipated to begin AGLS next year. Great, and we've had a lot going on in the past couple months.

So our wonderful AGLS coordinator, Chelsea Northman, I'm going to point her out, is here today with us. And we actually had our third meeting for our AGLS advisory committee. This committee is made up of community members, LCPS staff, students, so it's been really great to have her facilitate conversations and have them give input into the profile of an AGLS graduate, what experiences and curriculum we really want to roll out for our students, and

gathering feedback on a handbook for students that are new to the program, as well as give input into a summer bridge program. In terms of community outreach, we're really in our third round of admissions and have approximately 50% of our program filled at this time. I'm very excited about that. We will continue to offer seats through our weekly rounds until all of those possible seats are filled, and this will continue until the start of the school year.

In terms of spring events, we're scheduling visits for admitted students with the coordinator. She's also hosting office hours, parent meetings to review the handbook and program expectations, and a summer engagement activity for those admitted students. And our course progression, so we have looped in counseling, and started outreach for those upper-level DE courses, particularly in social science and world language. Awesome. Thank you, ladies. Next up is a high-level overview

of the authorization process at Parkview High School, where we're at, and then the career-related program that we are beginning the process at Loudoun Valley, Heritage, and Parkview as well. I'm going to turn it over to Grant Schaefer, who works intimately with all three of these schools. Hi. I'll start by just sharing a little bit of what we've done already here. Last year at this time, one of the main things we did is hire the IB coordinator for Parkview. It's Darcy Malone.

She comes to us from Fairfax with extensive experience in IB overall. We also had some trainings there, as you can see, with Dr. Jefferson, the principal, and myself. This year has involved the candidacy phase. Again, we have rising ninth graders who are in the portal right now, and we're going through that lottery process for those out-of-zone students. Teachers have been spending this year doing professional development that's

required as part of the process and starting to write their course outlines, which is required as well. Next year will be the consultation phase and the actual visit. We have a pre-visit scheduled for early June with our consultant that the IB provides for us in this process. We actually have more of the official visit that's going to happen in the fall of next year. And then we're going to

have those students through the lottery process now will be enrolling and starting in ninth grade at Parkview and getting them ready for those IB courses in junior and senior year. So, that's going to be happening, again, for out of zone in ninth and then Parkview only in 10th. One thing that is happening right now is going through and talking to current Parkview ninth graders to make them aware of IB,

essentially planting the seed for them to take courses in 11th grade when they are in 11th grade. So they can then choose to do that in the '27-28 school year. They can take courses, just singleton courses, or they can choose to do the full diploma program in the '27-28 school year. So we're starting that now, having those conversations with ninth graders. So moving on to more specifics there.

I'll highlight a couple things here. One is, again, the curriculum development piece. That's actually been helpful having Heritage and Valley already. So we can take a lot of that, and we're going to be offering those similar courses. So that has already been done. Professional development, we only have two content areas left that have not received that training yet. So we've done a good job on that

and, again, working with a consultant and the enrollment update of going through the lottery process right now and having those students both be offered seats and accept those seats and starting to understand more about what is life going to be like at Parkview, what does that look like in ninth and 10th grade, to make sure they have their VDOE required courses completed, but they're also ready to jump into that very full load that it takes to do the diploma program in 11th and 12th grade.

And so switching over to the career-related program, we wanted to give you a little bit of background on what is the career-related program. So, this is an aspect of IB, right? So, the way it relates to IB is that students who choose to do the career program would take two IB courses. So let's say, for example, English and History, right?

So they can take two of the core, and then they would be focused on the career-related program core, which would be the personal and professional skills course. A teacher is going to be trained in that, and that's a course very unique to the career program. They're going to take language development, which is essentially we want to make sure that they have a language background, so a language acquisition. The reflective project and service learning go hand-in-hand.

It really is about applying their knowledge in career-related learning to service and to tracking that. So it's similar to the IB core, which has a component called Community Activity and Service. It's essentially that, but in the CP component. So those are things that make the career program unique. A little bit of the timeline here, finishing up a

request for candidacy now, and we'll hear back from that hopefully next month. I have that scheduled for later this month. Then the candidacy phase would kick off next school year. We would be doing similar to what I shared earlier that Parkview's doing right now. It would look very similar with teachers getting trained, making sure that our policies are all aligned and that we're ready

to offer CP again in the '27-28 school year. Thank you, Mr. Schaefer. And now we'll transition into an update on our ROTC expansion for the Army branch. Shown here is the process we used in making the host school selection. This is the same process that has guided all of

our other academy decisions, ensuring fairness, transparency, and consistency across the division. We held a dedicated session with all high school principals to walk through the Army ROTC program. During that session, we covered the program goals, expectations, and what hosting would entail.High school principals then received an interest form and had until close of business on February 13th to indicate whether they wished to be considered as a host site.

A committee then reviewed all submissions using a clear set of criteria. The goal was to identify the school best positioned to support the academy's success. The school decision was guided by a thorough assessment of four key criteria. Community alignment, ensuring the academy is placed where community interest and demographic data shows strong support and relevance. Leadership commitment, confirming that school leadership not only expressed interest but demonstrated

readiness to champion and sustain the program. Building capacity, verifying that the school has the space, staffing flexibility, and infrastructure to host the academy without compromising existing programs. And then lastly, transportation and accessibility, selecting a location that provides reasonable access for students across the division. With that, we are happy to announce that the school selected was Stone Bridge High School, and we look forward to working with

Principal Dr. Flynn on this journey of bringing this program expansion to LCPS. And with that, I'm going to turn it over to Mrs. Domer for the next slide. Thank you. So for the JROTC expansion, while it's a valuable opportunity, starting a program is really challenging. It requires federal approval, a large and sustained enrollment, and often requires a multi-year wait due to limited national capacity.

A strong alternative is the National Defense Cadet Corps, or the NDCC. It offers the same focus on leadership, citizenship, and student development, but can be launched locally and much more quickly. The NDCC allows us to begin serving students now while building the foundation for the future of JROTC programs. In short, it's a practical first step that moves us forward without delay. And then over to Dr. Grots. Thank you, Ms. Domer.

Just a quick highlight. I'm not going to read through all these bullet points, but for the public, there is no difference. You would not notice any differences between an NDCC program and a JROTC program. As Ms. Domer mentioned, you can wait upwards of 20, 30, sometimes even 40 years to get a JROTC program. The route that we are sharing, most school systems are not aware that this is an opportunity to either fast-track a JROTC program or to give one a test run. One of the main differences is really the funding mechanism.

A cost-sharing opportunity, like a JROTC program, is where you split the bill with the service branch. With an NDCC, it is fully funded by the host school district. What does that mean? It means that we pay 100% of the instructor salaries. The military still picks up the textbooks and the curriculum, but everything else is largely identical. Students get the same advanced military ranking in terms of cadet

benefits. They still participate in competitive events like drill, color guard, marksmanship. One area that we try to navigate is that we are only bringing one instructor on, where if you look at the Navy program at County, there are three instructors. So you want to just pace yourself in terms of enrollment. The hope is, down the road, we would convert this program over to an official Army JROTC program where we would be eligible for a second or even a third instructor.

One of the enrollment criterias for an official JROTC program is 100 cadets or a minimum of 10% of your student population. With an NDCC, we have much more flexibility to maintain and not move into probationary status for being under-enrolled. Next slide, please. Just a quick overview of the timeline, '25, '26 has been a program and budget approval stage. We put in a budget proposal of a little over $300,000 to get the program up and running.

'26, '27 will be a planning year. We hope to recruit an instructor, to give that instructor an opportunity to begin recruitment, meeting with students, meeting with future cadets, and building out their program. '27, '28 would be year one. We would hope to enroll our grade nine students. In '28, '29, we would be welcoming our year two students for matriculation. Next slide, please. That's it.

Yep. That concludes, and we have lots of experts here for each program, so we're happy to answer any questions you might have. Thank you so much. It is very exciting to see all these things coming to fruition. I appreciate the updates on all of them. I will pass it to my colleague, Mr. Pepper, for his questions and comments first. Thank you- Assuming you have them ... Madam Chair. Oh, I've got a ton of questions. So I'm going to start with the Academy of Global Linguistic Studies and then work my way through IB and then just match the presentation.

So 100 students we're looking at enrollment. How many, just out of curiosity, have applied for the Academy of Global Linguistic Studies? Ooh, we're getting data. I see it. Do you think that could be pulling it up right now? All right. From the expert over here, I was going to pull it up, but 337 have applied. Okay. And we're hoping for up to 150 in each pathway. To enroll. We're approximately 25 in each pathway right now. We're in round three right now.

So can I ask, how are the rounds determined? What constitutes a first round, a second round, and so on? So it is a lottery program, so in the first round, it's just Monday through Thursday, we give that window of time. So it's a window for those students to accept or decline their offer. If they don't accept by that Thursday at 11:59 PM, then their seat expires. Oh, wow. And then the next week, we move on to the next appropriate student on the

wait list. So we continue to do that all the way up until the program's filled, or if we have a student move over the summer, then we would fill that seat as well. Super interesting. And I know that we're still building the profile of a graduate. And I don't know who this is really a question for, but what are you guys thinking in terms of a summer bridge program for this? Because I know that was mentioned.

So some of it is community building, so that these students are coming across the county or from all over the county to attend Dominion High School, so it's kind of getting them acclimated to that, introducing them to other students in the program, and building connections. And then getting them excited for what's ahead in terms of introductions to some of the courses and partnerships and things they'll be doing. So we're not thinking for a lengthy one. We know students have lots of commitments over the summer.

So around two days is what we're thinking at this point in time, and also an opportunity for them to meet some of the teachers. We are still in the process of hiring some fabulous teachers or recruiting some within Dominion to run some of these courses. Okay. So I saw that. I was like, "Oh, there's an engagement activity, and there's also a bridge." I was wondering if it was something along the lines of making sure writing skills or language skills, or to make sure that these students who are applying to the program have the skills to be successful in what appears

to be a pretty robust and exciting opportunity for a lot of our students. So, I wasn't sure it was more academic or social, but it appears to be more on the social side, which is fine, but just had some thoughts on that. I know there was some discussion. I think, Kelly, we could speak more about the language piece too, correct? Yeah. I think we're still in the planning process, but getting some students a little bit of exposure, at least to the cultural elements, just an introduction to get them, again, excited about learning that language. But the students, most of them are going to be coming in with zero background

knowledge or experience with the language. Okay. Do you want to do this one by one, Ms. Turnoff? Or do you want- You keep rolling. I'll just keep going with my list. All right. So I'll move on to IB. So I appreciate that. IB, first thing, this is totally an aside, but I want to give a shout-out to my former colleague, Darcie Malone Hood. Who, when I heard her name, I was like, "Oh, you hired somebody awesome who I've actually worked with" which is absolutely fantastic. Questions for the IB program, particularly at Park View.

I know you had mentioned that there are students who might attend Park View who are not in the program but want to take a singleton. Maybe a kid is really, really interested in psychology, and they want to take IB Psych. Is that something that any student can still do? Or is it once the program gets really up and going, is it then just limited to the students in the program? I can start off. We allow students currently at Heritage and Valley, so it'll be the same. They can take a singleton course at those two schools, so it'll be the same at Park View.

Okay. That's good to know. How many students is the number that we're looking for at Park View enrolled in the program? So for out of zone, we had allotted 30 seats for this initial- Okay ... to come in from out of zone, and then our in-zone students also applied, but they have access. But it just helps us keep track of who's interested in the full diploma so that we can ensure we are supporting them throughout the process.

And is that going to be geographical, so that, for example, students on the eastern end are, if they want to do IB there at Park View, and then sort of in the middle, they're going to be at Heritage, and then on the western side is Valley? Yeah. So they're zoned. So it's Potomac Falls, Dominion, Riverside, Broad Run, and Park View. Okay. And Stone Bridge. And Stone Bridge. Thank you. So it's Central and then Eastern Mountain that are zoned. Just trying to- Yeah ... geographic map in my head, and it wasn't being

totally perfect. And then question on what does the pre-IB, because I know you said we're going to do the pre-IB. As someone who's dearly familiar with IB, including the CP, what is the pre-IB looking like? I know that, at least in Falls Church, one of the things that we do for pre-IB is that we make sure that our World History 1 course, or World History 2, World History 1 gets shifted down to eighth grade, and then World History 2 gets shifted into ninth grade. I know that you know that. What is that going to look like?

Yeah. Well, you know a lot. Yeah. So it's that. It's making sure they have government as well. Mm-hmm. So it's a little bit of a switch for a few of those courses. And really, academically making sure they're ready to take on the load, as you know- Mm-hmm ... of IB. Another thing that we're doing as we're learning and we're growing IB is making sure that we're developing a cohort

type model so that these students can rely on each other and essentially start to build some of those executive functioning skills to make sure that they can be successful- Mm-hmm ... in the diploma program and using the theory of knowledge class when they get to 11th grade as sort of a de facto homeroom. Let me give you a couple plugs if I can. First thing that I would love to suggest for you guys, and I shouldn't be doing this, but is when the students,

particularly in the sciences, for example, I would recommend that it's not just the IB teachers who experience some of the IB training. It's the pre-IB teachers, right? Because there's a lot of things that students have to learn to speak the language and walk the walk and talk the talk as they get in IB. So even little things like, what does it look like to write an IB-style lab report? Or what does it look like to do an independent assessment, an IA? So that's the big thing. And then the TOK course, I love the idea of using it as a homeroom.

That's brilliant. I would also suggest strongly that the extended essay run through there if it's not already. That's a huge thing. As far as CP goes, so we'll switch little gears to CP. Told you I had a lot of questions. You're good. Those were me, so have at it. I know. As far as CP goes, for language, are we looking at a requirement where the students have to take a language at the school, or is it something where they can just... Because I know it's really just a log of hours.Are they able to do something

on their own, like a Duolingo or a Babbel? I know that in Falls Church, when we introduced the CP program, we allowed them to just log their hours using a Duolingo app. That's a good question. I can take it. I think we're still trying to work some of that out. Okay. And that was one thing I didn't really expand on is that's a logistic that we're working out, as well as the CTE courses that each school wants to offer.

So we'll start to work that out through the candidacy phase. But thank you for that. That's helpful. And then the other thing is when you talk about the course, I'm assuming that you're talking about the pathways we're going to offer in the CP program. Is that where you're... What are the pathways that we're going to offer? Correct. We want to include Dr. Grubbs and the CTE team to make sure that we're both in alignment with what CTE wants, but also looking at, we've already

looked at some data of what are the most popular CTE courses. This is also a way to engage some students in IB who may have thought that IB maybe wasn't for them, more accessible. Yeah. No, the CP program is fantastic. And then, so that's actually my last question on the IB program is who are we allowing to enroll? If there's a student who's outside perhaps one of the three schools, are they going to say, "I'm really interested in this pathway. I think this program might be for me." Is that something we're looking towards, or are we going to just keep it for those students who are already housed at Valley

and Heritage and Park View? So I'll start, and Grant can add in. The thought is we would still bring in our IB candidates in ninth grade, and in 11th grade, they would have a choice of continuing on to the CP or going for the full diploma. These are big decisions for our ninth graders coming in. Yeah, they are. And a lot of times, some of our kids get to junior year, and they realize maybe the full diploma wasn't... So they would have an option there, kind of like Hamsai, where

they pick a pathway at that point. So this would be very similar. We would bring them in still within the numbers of seats that we have available, and students would be able to select that pathway. And then students that are zoned for that school would have access to either the CP or the IB- Okay ... full diploma. Finally, I will move on to the JROTC type program, although it's not. I know that we mentioned that we're going to look to hire...

First, congratulations to Stonebridge, but look to hiring an instructor. Is that a challenging position to find someone to fill? Yeah. Great question. So just one step to clarify is that now that we've identified a site, we now submit an official application to the Army. We have had discussions. We feel like we have a really good justification and rationale. They will come out, and they'll do a site visit. The space over there meets the initial requirements of offering a JROTC, so we're not concerned with the space.

Once it's approved, then we work very closely with them on hiring an instructor. We chose Army very deliberately because traditionally the other three JROTC pathways are very challenging to hire. Marine Corps on the East Coast is a really tough program to recruit. I had five Marine Corps programs in my previous system. We had to close three of them down because we couldn't have a senior military instructor. We converted those to NNDCCs, National Navy Defense Cadet Corps, so there's always a backup plan.

But Army tends to be the ones that are easier to stand up. Also, in the last year and a half, the JROTC branches have reduced the licensure requirements to be a JROTC instructor. It used to be that you had to be retired military and have 20 years experience. I think it's down to eight years of experience with the Army or the armed service branch. So we feel very confident that in this region, we should have no issue finding an Army instructor. Great. Thank you very much. And Madam Chair, I think that's everything.

Thank you, Mr. Pepper. I had a lot of the same questions about enrollment and about hiring. And in that same vein, my questions really have to do with staffing. So as we're transitioning into this more pathways-based model, and we're starting to overlap some of these programs, I know Ms. Kelly has been at all of my committee meetings talking about the various branches of different things that are going on, which is very exciting. My question is, and this goes across all of the three that we've talked

about today, are we seeing that staffing is an issue? Are we concerned about that? Is there one area more than others? What does that look like in terms of incentivizing our teachers to take on these extra things? And then my last piece of that is what is the communication like to staff in terms of this transition for these schools so that they know it's coming and that those opportunities for them might exist?

So I'll start and then turn it over to Dr. Grubbs or Ms. Clark. In terms of... I thought I had one question, but you snuck in a couple there in there. So in terms of staffing, as we have been developing these special programs, we are learning, and we are being thoughtful about adding some additional staffing, primarily at the start of new programs. So, for example, the AGLS program, we're seeding that program with

the FTE for the two language teachers that are going to start next year at Dominion. We'll evaluate that over time in terms of enrollment and the needs of the school. Similarly, we learned maybe in our second or third year with IB that there were some additional supports that were needed to make sure that schools can run class sizes that initially may be small without having to take a pinch across the rest of their staffing. So as we're developing programs, we're becoming a little

bit more thoughtful about seeding some initial staffing when we go to the board with the proposal. And then new ideas may come. So like for example, we've had conversations at for Hamsai about do they need some support as they go to year three and four. Now, in terms of incentives, we've talked a little bit about this, soThere are, depending on the program need, we do build in some stipends. So for example, when we were initially developing

our IB programs, each school system gets an advisor, and they give you different models for what they do. You'll probably have an opinion on the advice we were given, Mr. Pepper, but do you give staffing or do you give stipends for certain roles? And so I'll ask Ms. Clark or Mr. Schaefer to talk a little bit about how we've done stipends for IB. And can you also talk a little bit about some of the curriculum development support we have for IB, for teachers knowing some of the extra lift that we give, how you work with the coordinators on that?

Yeah, absolutely. So, we do have some funding that was part of our initial proposal for professional development and curriculum development for each school. The coordinators are responsible for divvying up those hours amongst their teachers within their school. A lot of times those are just for IB meetings that they might have to hold after hours, after their contract. And then we've worked with each curriculum office as well. They are the ones that really work on the curriculum and for IB courses as well, all courses.

So they follow their SOP and their guidelines for that. But we do have those extra hours for those extra responsibilities, for working with students on their extended essay. That's very time-consuming and can be assigned for extra hours outside of the contract day. We also have stipends. We have an EE stipend, a CAS stipend, and a, what's the last one?

TOK stipend. Those individual stipend positions support the coordinator with really overseeing those three parts of the core. And then, for example, as Mr. Slevin mentioned, in our CP proposal, there is some staffing that was in that initial proposal that we were asking for that will be part of the budget next school year, going into the following year to support the expansion of CP at all three schools.

And then I'll turn it over to Dr. Grubbs to talk about ROTC. Sure. I think your initial question, I think staffing is always on our mind. There's so much happening in a school around enrollment numbers and class sizes, and I think it's something we really need to stay ahead of as a school system. I think in terms of Army and then our expansion plan, we built into the budget the funding for this instructor. So we were trying to get a little bit ahead of that. If we converted over, we would get support from the Army moving

forward. Jumping a little bit ahead to our expansion plan presentation, some of the initial phases, we're really looking at more of program conversions with existing staffing, right? Let's look at your enrollment, year one, year two. You're offering four or five CT courses that are significantly under-enrolled, maybe not a lot of student interest. How do we repurpose those FTEs and bring in a new program? We have an example. Ms. Alpers and I just spoke to today. We have a program,

low enrollment, low interest, that is an FTE that we're not utilizing very deliberately. We have plans to introduce an intro to health sciences program there in the next year or two. That's FTE neutral, and that's where we're looking really for year one and year two. Where I think we need to get ahead of is as we look at year three, year four, year five of our expansion plan, like bringing in an aircraft technology program, we are going to need some additional FTEs because we will have been FTE neutral to that point. And I know Mr.

Sackett will be more than willing to take those FTEs down the road. So does that help? Does that- Yeah, I think that's a very thoughtful answer and a thoughtful approach. I want us to be aligned with the vision, but I also want to make sure we're being mindful of what, especially as board members, what is going to be expected to build in as we expand. Sure. And correct me if I'm wrong, but I think in the past, there have been some things

at the academies that have been not able to go on or have been a struggle to continue because of specialized staffing. And so I just want to make sure that we're not going to keep having these drop-offs if we can't get the people that we need. Absolutely. And so I'm very appreciative, and Mr. Sackett and I had a long conversation about stretching those FTEs and finding those efficiencies, and so I'm really grateful for that collaboration. And then just back to IB, I am hearing from some teachers, I'll be honest, I put

this on Mr. Slevin's radar. Heritage sits in my district, so I do hear from people from time to time that as this program, as they're getting more in-depth with it, they want to do more. They love the program. That's not the issue. The issue is in order to do that, the sustainability with the workload and pouring into the kids and the curriculum and specializing it for each learner and their different projects and things that they do. It sounds like there's rumblings

of needing some more support in terms of incentivizing teachers, and that would be monetarily. They are grateful that they have their PD paid for, and I know there's additional things that they have covered, but I think that as we're getting better, so to speak, at IB, there is starting to be that, is it worth it?
